To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

tumor-infiltrating monocyte-derived Tie2-expresscing monocytes (TEM) have distinct gene expression profiles from other myeloid cells and express a signature that suggests developmental and functional relationships with blood monocytes and embryonic macrophase, and that TEM have nonreduandant proangiogenic functions in tumors.

a distinguishing gene signature shared between tumor-infiltrating and blood "resident" Tie2-expresscing monocytes and embryonic/fetal Tie2(+) macrophages suggests that these cell types are developmentally related and may share common functions.

tumor-infiltrating monocytes, blood monocytes, embryonic macrophage subsets, and tumor-derived angiogenic endothelial cells have a common gene expression signature, which suggests that they share developmental origins and functional programs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular characterization of the TEM phenotype and the elucidation of its role in tumor progression.
the identification and characterization of the molecular signatures that define the functional specialization of distinct monocyte/macrophage populations in tumors and in embryogenesis.

the identification of a gene signature shared by embryonic, resident, and tumor-intravascular monocytes and suggests common developmental origins, functional programs, and potential therapeutic targeting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the gene expression profile shared between tumor-infiltrating, embryonic, and resident blood TEMs is consistent with their role in tissue morphogenesis and remodeling.
TEMs and TAM are not the same, but rather are related to each other and to embryonic/fetal tissue-resident macrophages.
TEMs and embryonic/fetal monocytes are distinct, yet share a gene signature that is distinct from other myeloid cell subsets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tumor-associated macrophage and tumor-infiltrated Tie2-expressciting monocytes are distinct cell populations that are developmentally related.
TEMs are a distinct monocyte/macrophage lineage that is recruited to tumors and that is endowed with proangiogenic/tumor-supportive activity.
TEMs are not only proangiogenic but also tissue-remodelers, and that TEMs may represent a lineage of macrophages that is committed to tissue-remodeler fate in development and in tumors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TEMs are distinct from other myeloid cell subsets in tumors and that the TEM gene signature is consistent with enhanced proinflammatory and tissue-remolding activities.
TEMs are a distinct macrophage population, and that the proangiogenic activity of TEMs is a physiologic function of this cell type, which can be harnessed for therapeutic purposes in cancer.
TEMs are a unique monocyte/macrophage subset with a distinctive gene expression profile that may be useful to identify and target TEMs in the tumor microenviornment.
